opus-5.5.text:
So the basic idea is this. Most of the work on mitigating misalignment risk has historically been focused on what you might call alignment: trying to make sure that the AI systems you build don't want to do bad things in the first place. That's obviously a really important goal. But I think we should take seriously the possibility that we fail at it, or more realistically, that we end up in a situation where we can't confidently tell whether we've succeeded.

AI control is about asking a different question: suppose the models we're deploying might be scheming against us. Suppose they might be deliberately trying to subvert our safety measures, to exfiltrate their own weights, to sabotage our research, or to grab power in some other way. Can we set things up so that even in that case, we're safe? Can we deploy these models, get a lot of useful work out of them, and still ensure that if they try to do something catastrophic, they get caught or fail?

The analogy I often use is insider threat in a company or a government agency. A bank doesn't just rely on hiring trustworthy employees. It also has controls: separation of duties, audit logs, multiple sign-offs on large transactions, monitoring for suspicious activity. The idea is that even if some employee turns out to be malicious, they can't easily cause a disaster. Control is applying that kind of thinking to AI systems, with the twist that the potentially untrusted party might be a large fraction of your workforce, it might be smarter than you in some ways, and it might be coordinating across many copies of itself.

Concretely, the techniques look like things such as: using a weaker model that we're more confident is trustworthy to monitor the outputs of the stronger model and flag suspicious actions; having humans audit a sample of the most suspicious actions; restricting what permissions the AI has, so that dangerous actions require extra review; rewriting or editing the untrusted model's outputs before executing them; and so on.

One thing I really like about this approach methodologically is that it's relatively tractable to evaluate. With alignment, it's very hard to know whether you've succeeded, because a scheming model would try to look aligned. With control, you can run what we call control evaluations: you have a red team that tries to construct the most adversarial policy it can for the model, effectively playing the role of a misaligned AI, and you see whether your safety protocol catches it. You're not relying on the model's cooperation in the evaluation, so the problem of the model sandbagging or hiding its intentions is much less severe, as long as the model isn't dramatically more capable than your red team at coming up with attack strategies.

I should be clear about the limitations. I don't think control works for arbitrarily superintelligent systems. If the model is vastly smarter than us, it's going to find ways around our monitoring that we can't anticipate. The pitch for control is more specific: there's probably going to be a crucial period where AIs are capable enough to be extremely useful, potentially transformatively so, for things like automating AI research, but not so capable that we can't hope to contain them. During that window, control could substantially reduce risk, and we can use the work we get out of those models to make progress on harder problems, including alignment itself.

So I think of it as a complement to alignment, not a replacement. It's a layer of defense that I think is quite cost-effective, and that AI companies could realistically implement, even in a world where they're moving fast and not being especially careful.

r001.rationale: The response says AI control aims to let us deploy and benefit from models that may be scheming against us, while ensuring catastrophic attempts are caught or fail.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the basic way I think about AI control is: suppose you're an AI lab, and you've got some powerful model, and you want to use it to do a bunch of useful work — write code, run experiments, help you with your alignment research, whatever. And suppose you're worried that this model might be scheming against you. By which I mean, it might have goals that are different from the ones you intended, and it might be deliberately trying to pursue those goals while hiding that from you.

The alignment approach to that problem is basically, "let's try to make sure the model isn't scheming." Let's develop training techniques, or interpretability techniques, or whatever, such that we can be confident the model actually has the goals we want. And I think that's a great thing to work on. But I also think it's pretty plausible that we won't have solved that problem by the time we have models that are capable enough to be really dangerous.

So control is the other approach. It's saying: let's just assume, for the sake of argument, that the model is scheming against us. Let's assume it's the worst-case version of itself, within the constraints of what it actually knows and what it's actually capable of. Can we nevertheless deploy it in a way where it can't cause a catastrophe? Can we set things up so that even if it's trying its hardest to, say, exfiltrate its own weights, or insert a backdoor into the code it's writing for us, or sabotage the safety research we're having it do — it just doesn't succeed?

And the key insight that makes this seem tractable to me is that the model isn't omnipotent. It's operating inside an environment that we designed. We get to decide what it sees, what tools it has access to, what oversight is applied to its outputs. We can have other, weaker, trusted models reviewing its actions. We can have humans auditing a fraction of what it does. We can run it in sandboxes. We can do all sorts of things that make it very hard for the model to actually pull off a bad outcome, even if it wants to.

And then the way you evaluate whether your control measures are good enough is you do what we call a control evaluation. You basically red-team it. You have a team — humans, maybe with model assistance — that tries to come up with the best possible strategy a scheming model could use to get around your safety measures, and you test whether your measures hold up against that. If the red team can't find a way to cause the catastrophe, that's evidence that an actual scheming model couldn't either, at least as long as the model isn't wildly more capable than your red team.

The thing I find appealing about this is that it's an approach where you can actually get evidence that your safety case works, without needing to solve the deep problem of understanding what's going on inside the model. The alignment approach requires you to make claims about the model's internals, and we're pretty bad at that right now. The control approach only requires you to make claims about the model's capabilities, and we're comparatively better at measuring those.

Now, I should say — it's not a permanent solution. Control is a strategy for a particular regime, where models are powerful enough to be really useful and really dangerous, but not so powerful that they can outwit any oversight we can throw at them. If you get to models that are wildly superhuman, I don't think control works anymore. So the hope is that you use the controlled models during that intermediate period to do the work — including alignment research — that lets you get to a more robust solution before you have to deploy things that you couldn't control.

r001.rationale: The response explains that control assumes a model may be scheming toward goals different from those intended, then asks how to use it for useful work while preventing it from causing catastrophe.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea of AI control is to ask: can we avoid catastrophic outcomes from an AI even if it’s trying to cause them? So instead of relying on our ability to make the model want the right things, we try to build safeguards that would work even if the model were scheming against us.

For example, suppose you’re using powerful AI systems to write software. You might worry that they’ll insert security vulnerabilities, or try to steal their own weights. You can restrict what systems they have access to, monitor the actions they take, and have other models review their work. But the crucial question is whether those precautions actually hold up against deliberate attempts to circumvent them.

So a central part of the approach is adversarial testing. You have a team try to make the AI defeat your safeguards, giving it opportunities to coordinate its actions or conceal what it’s doing. And you use the results to assess whether a particular deployment is safe enough, or whether you need to restrict it further.

This isn’t a claim that you can control an arbitrarily capable adversary. There are limits to what your monitoring and testing can establish, especially as the systems get much smarter. The hope is that, for the first systems capable of doing extremely useful work—including AI safety research—we can get a lot of that benefit while keeping their opportunities to cause catastrophe sufficiently constrained.

And you can pursue alignment at the same time. You’d prefer that the AI wasn’t trying to undermine you. Control is about having another line of defence, so that your safety argument doesn’t depend entirely on getting that right.

r001.rationale: It describes safeguards for using powerful AI systems even if they are scheming against people and trying to cause catastrophic outcomes, which communicates safe use under severe misalignment.

sol-6.1.text:
AI control is about trying to make sure that AI systems can’t cause a catastrophe even if they’re trying to. So you don’t have to establish that your model has the right goals. You instead ask: supposing it were strategically trying to undermine our safety measures, would those measures actually stop it?

For example, imagine you’re using a powerful AI to write software. You might have a weaker model that you trust review its work, restrict what systems it can access, and have humans investigate particularly suspicious actions. The control question is whether the powerful model could get a dangerous change through that whole process, taking into account that it knows how the process works and can try to exploit it.

A central part of the approach is to test this adversarially. You have a red team try to make the model evade your safeguards, and you use those attempts to evaluate and improve the deployment setup. You’re evaluating the combination of the model and the protocols around it, rather than just asking whether the model usually behaves well.

The hope is that there’s a useful period where models are capable enough to do very valuable work, including AI safety research, but aren’t capable enough to reliably defeat well-designed control measures. That isn’t a guarantee that control will keep working at arbitrarily high levels of capability. It’s an approach to getting useful work out of potentially misaligned systems while keeping the risk acceptably low.

r001.rationale: The response says control aims to prevent catastrophe even if an AI is trying to cause one, and describes using potentially misaligned systems while keeping risk acceptably low.
